DecKeywords: White finger disease; Reconsideration (consideration of evidence); Vibrations (tools); Words and phrases (latency)
DecSummary: The worker's request to reconsider Decision No. 1260/87 was granted.  In Decision No. 1260/87, the original hearing panel denied entitlement for white finger disease which the worker claimed resulted from use of vibratory tools in his work as a driller.  There was a misunderstanding of the evidence as a result of many different interpretations given to the term latency.  There were references to latency from time of first exposure to onset of symptoms and to latency from last exposure to onset of symptoms.  The specialist involved was also concerned that his general non-specific answers to questions on latency were used to make a decision regarding the worker's condition.

DecKeywords: Presumptions (entitlement) (burden of proof); Presumptions (entitlement) (standard of proof); Reconsideration (dissent); Reconsideration (error of law)
DecSummary: The worker requested reconsideration of Decision No. 88/87, in which entitlement for a stroke was denied.  The majority of the original hearing panel found that employment did not make a significant contribution to the stroke.  The majority stated that, since it made its decision on the balance of probabilities, it was not necessary to rely on the presumption clause, but even if the presumption clause were applicable, there was sufficient medical evidence to rebut it.  The dissenting panel member stated that the presumption always applied but its effect would vary from case to case.  In this case, the dissenting panel member found that the presumption was not rebutted.

DecKeywords: Class of employer; Jurisdiction, Board (class of employer); Jurisdiction, Tribunal (class of employer)
DecSummary: The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer regarding its rate group for 1985.  The employer was in the business of supplying labour to industry.  As a result of an audit in 1984, it was reclassified from janitorial service Rate #907 to business of supplying labour other than clerical Rate #854, retroactive to 1981.  On appeal, the Board exercised its discretion and applied Rate #854 only from January 1, 1985.  In 1986, as a result of a request by an employer trade association, the Board transferred all firms engaged in the supply of labour other than clerical from Rate #854 to the lower Rate #656.

DecKeywords: Damages, contribution or indemnity; Leasing company; Right to sue; Supplier of motor vehicle, machinery or equipment
DecSummary: The Panel determined the application of s.8(10) to the defendant leasing company, which was the lessor of the vehicle involved in a motor vehicle accident.  The Panel considered the applicability of Ling v. Transamerica and Munro v. Gibb.

DecSummary: Worker suffered compensable accident in which he fell and strained his back and neck.  Worker also suffering from psychological problems.     Worker entitled to benefits for psychological condition.  Accident may not have been the cause of the psychological problems but it at least triggered the reaction.  The accident was a significant contributing factor to development of the disabling psychological problem in a 'frail spirit'.

DecKeywords: Temporary total disability
DecSummary: Worker suffered compensable knee injury in April 1984, returned to work in August and laid off again in December 1984.  From December 1984 to March 1985, the Hearings Officer granted 50% temporary partial disability benefits.

DecKeywords: Continuity (of complaint); Disc, herniated; Significant contribution (of compensable accident to subsequent disability)
DecSummary: Worker suffered compensable back sprain in October 1981, as well as several other prior compensable back injuries.

DecKeywords: Continuing entitlement
DecSummary: The worker suffered a low back strain in January 1983.  She sought continuing benefits beyond July 1983.  Despite the lack of positive x-ray or laboratory test findings, the pain did not resolve.

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, statutory (use of material); Jurisdiction, Tribunal (access to worker file)
DecSummary: After a hearing, the Hearings Officer requested further medical information prior to rendering a decision.  The worker objected to release of the information to the employer.

DecKeywords: Disablement (unaccustomed strain)
DecSummary: Worker had been a meat wrapper for 12 years prior to lay-off for back condition.

DecKeywords: Hearing loss; Notice of accident (industrial disease); Notice of hearing; Parties
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Appeals Adjudicator denying entitlement for hearing loss. DecKeywords: Hearing loss; Investigation by Tribunal; Medical opinion (hearing loss); Steelworker

DecKeywords: Psychotraumatic disability; Temporary disability (beyond pension level)

DecKeywords: Chronic pain
DecSummary: The worker suffered a low back injury in November 1980 and received benefits until February 1982.  The worker appealed denial of benefits after February 1982.

DecKeywords: Alcoholism; Exposure (solvents) (white gasoline); Medical opinion (seizures)
DecSummary: The worker, while at home, sustained a seizure causing anoxia (a deficiency of oxygen) and resulting in brain damage described as post-anoxic encephalopathy.  The worker had symptoms of cardiac arrythmia caused by a syncopal seizure.  The worker claimed that the seizure resulted from his exposure to toxic solvents at work.

DecKeywords: Access to worker file, P. D.; Procedure (Practice Direction No. 1)
DecSummary: It was appropriate for the Tribunal Counsel Office to make the preliminary selection of material that is considered relevant to the appeal.  A Panel of the Tribunal would consider and determine objections to that selection.

DecKeywords: Second Injury and Enhancement Fund {SIEF}; Suitable employment; Psychogenic pain; Delay (onset of symptoms); Rehabilitation, vocational (program not offered by Board); Worker (long term service)
DecSummary: The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting benefits beyond October 1984 and granting 50% SIEF relief.  The worker was a punch press operator who suffered a fractured ankle in a compensable fall in February 1984.

DecSummary: An overhead crane operator was entitled to benefits for a low back condition related to exposure to vibrations as a crane operator for over 20 years.  The crane rolled on steel wheels over a steel track.  The evidence established that there was considerable vibration caused by heavy loads and uneven abutments of the rails.  The injuring process was the herniation and degeneration of the lower spine occurring over a period of time.

DecKeywords: Chondromalacia (knee); Recurrences (compensable injury)
DecSummary: Worker suffered compensable contusion of right knee when she slipped and fell in November 1980.  She returned to work in July 1981 and was off work for a recurrence in March and April 1982.

DecKeywords: Aggravation (preexisting condition) (mental condition); Continuing entitlement; Psychotraumatic disability
DecSummary: The worker suffered compensable injuries in January 1974 and August 1979.  After the second accident, she was laid off permanently in April 1980.  She received benefits until September 1980.

DecKeywords: Adjournment (additional evidence)

DecKeywords: Delay (onset of symptoms)

DecKeywords: Commutation (business investment)
DecSummary: Worker, living in Ontario, sought partial commutation of pension in order to renovate family homestead in Newfoundland as a business investment.

DecKeywords: Accident (occurrence); Credibility; Disablement (nature of work)
DecSummary: The worker laid off on December 21, 1984, claiming a chest disability.  He claimed this was an aggravation of a chest condition that first appeared during two days in May 1982 when he was working a lot of overtime.  There was a delay in treatment after May 1982 until November 1982 and no time off until February 1983.  On the morning of the lay-off in 1984, the worker had a serious confrontation with his employer.

DecKeywords: Availability for employment (job search); Rehabilitation (cooperation)
DecSummary: Tool and die maker suffered compensable shoulder strain in March 1985.

DecKeywords: Supplements, temporary (rehabilitative purpose)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying a temporary supplement to the worker's pension beyond September 1984.  By that date, the worker had been receiving the supplement for approximately 42 months.  The Board had supplied rehabilitation services and retraining.

DecKeywords: Continuity (of treatment); Rehabilitation (considering self totally disabled); Temporary partial disability
DecSummary: Worker suffered compensable shoulder disability in April 1964.  Lack of treatment or complaint from 1970 to 1985.  Board granted 50% benefits from February 1985 to July 1985 and 100% benefits thereafter.

DecKeywords: Adjournment (judicial review); Continuing entitlement; Medical examination (employer request); Psychotraumatic disability; Procedure (medical examination) (employer request) (application and merits together)
DecSummary: The worker suffered a wrist injury in December 1981.  The worker appealed a decision of the Appeals Adjudicator denying benefits subsequent to March 1983.

DecKeywords: Aggravation (preexisting condition) (disc, degeneration)

Panel admitted statement by another worker in response to oral testimony of witness.

DecKeywords: Delay (claim); Disablement (change in work)

DecSummary: Worker's representative requested adjournment since actual representative had prior commitment, of which Tribunal had been informed two months earlier.  Panel reviewed Tribunal guidelines for adjournment and denied request on grounds that there were not exceptional circumstances.

DecKeywords: Benefit of the doubt; Reconsideration (consideration of evidence)

DecSummary: Over 24 years of employment, miner had three and one-half years continuous exposure to stoper drill, five years of exposure to Sullivan 50 platform drill, ten years of continuous exposure to diamond drill and ten years of intermittent exposure to jack-leg and plugger drills at average rate of 15 to 30 minutes per day.

DecKeywords: Reconsideration (new evidence) (test)
DecSummary: The worker requested the reconsideration of a Tribunal decision which refused her leave to appeal a decision of the Appeal Board.  The Appeal Board decision denied the worker further benefits on the basis that the evidence failed to establish a continuing organic disability.

After each of these occurrences he returned to his regular employment as a machine operator.

DecSummary: A caretaker suffered compensable back, neck and shoulder injuries in 1977 and 1978.  The Board granted benefits for lay-offs until October 1981. DecKeywords: Procedure (addendum) (clarification of decision)
DecSummary: Clarification of Panel's intention in Decision No. 1150/87I that Board have opportunity to consider new evidence regarding fibrositis and chronic pain.

DecKeywords: Continuing entitlement; Consequences of injury (altered gait) (brace); Continuity (of treatment); Medical report (varying diagnoses); Rehabilitation, medical (cooperation)

DecKeywords: Administrative Fund (transfer of costs); Jurisdiction, Tribunal (transfer of costs); Referral to Board; Second Injury and Enhancement Fund {SIEF} (transfer of costs); Transfer of costs

In Decision No. 1260/87, the hearing panel denied entitlement for white finger disease.  The hearing panel did not accept expert medical opinion since the opinion was based on facts different than those found by the hearing panel.  In Decision No. 1260/87R, the reconsideration panel accepted the Ombudsman's conclusion that it was unreasonable for the hearing panel not to have requested a clarification from the expert.  The reconsideration panel got the clarification but found that the clarification was in accord with the original decision.

DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Appeals Adjudicator denying benefits beyond July 24, 1983 for shoulder and neck disabilities suffered in a compensable accident on July 12, 1983.

The worker was employed as a cook for a railway gang in an isolated location.  The worker claimed that she was sexually assaulted by the foreman and that she suffered the shoulder injury during the assault.  Several days later, the crew left the bush location and went to a small town.  After several days the crew returned to the town where the worker's supervisor was located.  She then reported the incident.  The foreman was charged with sexual assault but was acquitted due to insufficient evidence.

DecKeywords: Delay (treatment); Hearing (observers)
DecSummary: Worker objected to presence of two people from employer company at hearing. Employer has right to observe proceedings, but in circumstances, one person was sufficient.

DecSummary: Worker's employment as package maker banding steel coils involved repetitive movements of kind associated in medical literature with development of tennis elbow. The Appeal Board appeared to rely on the opinion of the WCB's medical consultants without setting out the basis for rejecting evidence of the worker's doctors that the continuing condition was related to the compensable accident and a medical text suggesting that occupational stress could result in the symptoms of this condition.

DecKeywords: Cancer (bladder); Exposure (beta-naphthylamine)
DecSummary: The worker sought entitlement to benefits for bladder cancer diagnosed in 1980.  For two years, during 1948 to 1950, he worked for a large rubber manufacturer.  During that period, the worker came into contact with Agerite White, an anti-oxidant that contained beta-naphthylamine (BNA).

DecKeywords: Disablement (nature of work)
DecSummary: Worker not entitled to benefits for back condition. No evidence of onset of low back disability during period when worker alleged gradual onset of pain. No evidence of disability from back condition during period for which worker claiming benefits.

DecKeywords: Availability for employment (reassessment of negative decision) (onus of proof); Availability for employment (reassessment of negative decision) (standard of proof); Rehabilitation (reassessment of negative decision) (onus of proof); Rehabilitation (reassessment of negative decision) (standard of proof)
DecSummary: The worker failed to accept suitable work in May 1982.  The Appeal Board disentitled the worker to temporary disability benefits, rehabilitation expenditures and supplementary pension benefits for periods from then to the date of its decision in May 1984.  In Decision No. 595/87L, the Tribunal granted leave to appeal on the issue of how long the disqualification should continue.

DecKeywords: Benefit of the doubt; Continuing entitlement; Intervening causes
DecSummary: Evidence showed that worker complained of back pain to his doctors only after non-work-related accidents occurring in February 1979 and October 1983. Evidence did not establish that worker's low back disability subsequent to October 1983 resulted from 1978 compensable accident.

DecKeywords: Availability for employment (reassessment of negative decision) (onus of proof); Availability for employment (reassessment of negative decision) (standard of proof); Reconsideration (error of law); Rehabilitation (reassessment of negative decision) (onus of proof); Rehabilitation (reassessment of negative decision) (standard of proof)
DecSummary: The Panel reconsidered Decision No. 595/87.  In 1984, the Appeal Board determined that the worker was partially, rather than totally, disabled from May 1982 to June 1982 and that the worker refused suitable work with no wage loss in May 1982.  However, it found that the worker was totally disabled from June 1982 to July 1982.  The Appeal Board found that the worker was disentitled to all temporary partial benefits subsequent to May 1982.  In Decision No. 595/87L, the Tribunal granted leave to appeal with respect to the finding that the worker was disentitled to all benefits subsequent to May 1982.  In Decision No. 595/87, the Hearing Panel stated that when a worker seeks reassessment of a negative decision regarding cooperation or availability, the onus is on the worker to bring forward clear and convincing evidence of a distinct change in approach.

DecKeywords: Delay (onset of symptoms); Psychotraumatic disability
DecSummary: Having regard to nature of accident suffered in January 1982, lack of medical treatment for neck condition until June 1982 and medical reports, worker's neck condition did not arise out of 1982 compensable accident. Medical evidence did not support finding of psychotraumatic condition. Worker's appeal denied.

DecKeywords: Preexisting condition; Temporary total disability
DecSummary: The employer appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer granting the worker entitlement to temporary total disability benefits for a period from December 13, 1984 when the worker suffered a lower back injury at work until March 4, 1985.  Coincidentally, the worker was summoned to a pension examination on January 30, 1985 and was awarded a 10% pension in relation to an earlier compensable accident.

DecKeywords: Disablement (strenuous work)
DecSummary: Ongoing work process not awkward or strenuous due to constant rest periods. Having regard to nature of work, absence of medical evidence relating disability to work and questionable evidence given by worker, work did not make significant contribution to disability.

DecKeywords: Delay (onset of symptoms)
DecSummary: Worker fell from top of truck in June 1984 and suffered hip and leg injuries.

DecKeywords: Accident (occurrence); Credibility
DecSummary: Not established that worker injured knee by banging it against table at work. Most probable cause of condition was injury sustained outside work. Worker not entitled to benefits. Allegation, that worker attempted to enlist co-worker to provide false information, could not be proved, therefore matter not taken into account in assessing credibility.

DecKeywords: Firefighter; Heart attack
DecSummary: Firefighter suffered heart attack and died while inspecting fire location.

DecKeywords: Delay (claim)

Worker did suffer back disability for which he received company sickness and accident benefits, but not established that disability arose out of and in the course of employment.

DecKeywords: Continuity (of treatment); Jurisdiction, Tribunal (final decision of Board)

DecKeywords: Continuity (of complaint)

Evidence showed no mention of any complaints, reporting, symptoms or treatment of worker's cervical condition until four months after compensable injury to lower back in 1985. No causal relationship established.

DecSummary: Worker not entitled to benefits for treatment for degenerative disc disease in 1984. Worker had pre-existing degenerative condition and significant accident prior to first of compensable accidents. Compensable accidents had been accepted as exacerbations of pre-existing condition. Medical opinion did not suggest that compensable aggravations had permanent effect on condition.

DecKeywords: Continuing entitlement; Incarceration

DecKeywords: Continuity (of treatment); Preexisting condition (osteoarthritis)

DecKeywords: Adjournment (illness of family member)

DecKeywords: Continuity (of complaint)

DecKeywords: Continuity (of treatment); Credibility (delay); Delay (appeal)

There was no specific incident, but rather a gradual progression to the point where the worker could no longer continue working.  The worker appealed the denial of entitlement to health care benefits in 1976 and the denial of total temporary disability benefits in 1978.

DecKeywords: Consequences of injury (insomnia); Depression; Preexisting condition (mental condition); Significant contribution (of compensable accident to psychological condition); Temporary disability (beyond pension level)

DecKeywords: Leave to appeal (substantial new evidence) (medical report)
DecSummary: The worker brought an application for leave to appeal a decision of the Appeal Board.  The Tribunal found that the medical report submitted by an ophthalmologist who examined the worker constituted substantial new evidence.  The Tribunal noted that the report, which set out detailed criticism of the diagnostic approach taken by other physicians who had examined the worker and gave a lengthy analysis in support of the ophthalmologist's finding of a different diagnosis, added substantially to the information available regarding the worker's condition.

DecKeywords: In the course of employment (employer's premises); In the course of employment (proceeding to and from work)
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying entitlement for a fall sustained by the worker outside her employer's units in an industrial mall.  The worker fell on the way to work on an unshovelled area immediately in front of and leading to the employer's door.

Over the next several months, the worker noticed a swelling in her left shoulder which was apparently successfully treated by ultrasound.  But in September 1981, the worker experienced an acute onset of pain with swelling over her left sternoclavicular joint.  From that point on this condition continued to best the worker.

DecSummary: In Decision No. 59/87, the Panel stated that the worker was entitled to total permanent disability benefits for psychological disability subsequent to October 1985.  The use of the word 'total' created an ambiguity.  It was not the Panel's intention to assess the worker's permanent disability.  The Panel intended to grant a permanent, as opposed to a provisional, award, but did not intend to determine the level of disability.  The Panel clarified the decision by removing the word 'total' and adding that the Board should determine the permanent disability rating.  [5 pages]

The Appeal Board accepted the opinion of the Board doctor over that of the worker's treating psychiatrist.  However, the Board doctor's report contained a factual error in stating that there was no evidence of any acute or chronic condition that could reasonably be related to employment, whereas in fact the treating psychiatrist's report contained a good deal of such evidence.  Further, the Appeal Board stated that the human rights commission had concluded that the worker may have been discriminated against, whereas in fact the worker's complaint of discrimination was substantiated.  This factual error could have led the Appeal Board to discount the effect of the worker's employment on her condition.

The refusal of access in the original decision was based on the fact that the employer appeared to be raising two different issues, one being SIEF relief and ongoing entitlement, the other being initial entitlement.  Different medical reports might thus have been relevant to the different issues.

The Panel member representative of workers was a senior official of the union to which the worker belongs.  The employer submitted that there was a perception of bias.  In order not to delay a decision on the merits, the Panel rescheduled the hearing before a differently composed Panel, while considering the objection.

Accordingly, if the worker's employment situation were to be negatively affected by the release of the medical file, he would have to seek a remedy against the employer in another forum. DecKeywords: Hearing loss
DecSummary: It was found to be more probable than not that the worker's employment was not a significant contributing factor to his bilateral sensori-neural hearing loss and tinnitus.  The glass company where he worked from 1971 to 1981 was noisy and he was exposed to high levels of noise for certain periods of time.  But he suffered no significant hearing loss in that time (five decibels), his hearing loss may have been caused by non-compensable factors such as aging and drugs, and it was unlikely that the tinnitus was caused by this employment since it started only a few months after he began work.  Individual susceptibility was not an operative factor in this case.  In light of these findings, it was not necessary to make an definitive finding regarding the levels of hazardous noise exposure at the plant.  The panel noted the point made in Decision No. 425 that it is not necessary for the last employer to be responsible for all of the exposure which resulted in hearing loss for a claim to be compensable.  But in this case there was no evidence that the hearing loss was attributable to exposure to hazardous noise while employed elsewhere.  In fact, the worker specifically denied being exposed to hazardous noise at any of his previous jobs.

The worker's subjective evidence, her medical condition at the time the work was attempted, her efforts to perform the work, the effects of these efforts on her, and the opinion of the examining family doctor, were also factors to be considered.

DecKeywords: Temporary partial disability; Temporary total disability
DecSummary: The worker appealed a decision of the Hearings Officer denying total disability benefits subsequent to February 1982.  The worker suffered compensable low back injuries in 1977 and 1979.  In February 1980 she was awarded a 20% pension.  In February 1982 her benefits were reduced to the pension level.  In January 1985, her pension was increased to 30% and she was awarded temporary partial 50% benefits retroactive to February 1982.  The Tribunal found that there is no clear demarcation line between categories of disability in the Act, and it would be misleading to suggest one.  It is necessary to look at all the facts and determine, in the context of the Act, where on the spectrum of disability the worker is during the time in question.  The fact that a worker is unemployable given the market does not mean that a worker is totally disabled.  However, where a worker might be able to do light work in the most controlled of settings, but could not hold down even a part-time job, the worker could still be considered totally disabled.  There is a fine line between these two situations.

DecKeywords: Adjournment (additional issues); Issue setting; Jurisdiction, Tribunal (final decision of Board); Jurisdiction, Tribunal (leave to appeal)
DecSummary: The worker appealed the 1979 decision of the Appeals Adjudicator.  As a preliminary matter, the employer's representative challenged the Tribunal's jurisdiction to hear the appeal on the basis that there was no final decision from the highest appeal level potentially available to the worker.  The employer argued therefore that the worker was obliged to bring application for leave to appeal.  The Tribunal rejected the employer's argument, stating that the precondition to the exercise of the Tribunal's jurisdiction set out in section 86g(2) requires only that the worker has received a final decision from the Board at the time the worker comes before the Tribunal.  If the worker cannot proceed further under the Board's own procedures then the worker has received a final decision and the Tribunal has jurisdiction.  As the worker had clearly received a final decision, the Tribunal had jurisdiction to hear the worker's appeal.

DecKeywords: Causation (thin skull doctrine); Consequences of injury (iatrogenic illness) (medication); Depression; Psychotraumatic disability; Preexisting condition (personality weakness); Significant contribution (of compensable accident to psychological condition)
DecSummary: The industrial accident involving a head injury of May 1981 was a significant contributing factor in the development of the worker's psychiatric disability as indicated by three factors.  (1) There was a temporal connection between the accident, the onset of symptoms and the development of the disability.  The worker exhibited mild indicators of emotional distress two months after the accident and was referred to a psychiatrist on suspicion of post-traumatic neurosis a year later.  (2) Though there was a preexisting personality weakness which rendered the worker more susceptible to this disability than the average worker, evidence of prior normal functioning minimized the theory of some dormant psychiatric illness brewing beneath the surface which was solely accountable for the disability during the period from 1982 to 1986.  But neither of these factors would have been sufficient without (3) a convincing medical opinion that persistent pain and inability to return to work precipitated the onset of depressive neurosis.

A computer print-out and other employer evidence indicated that the worker spent at most one third of his time between 1962 and 1981 scarfing, instead of most of his time as he testified.  A 1963 compensation claim based on a complaint that scarfing was hurting his arms was turned down.  He testified to minor problems from then until 1980, but lost no time and sought no medical attention, even after these problems became a little worse in 1975.  In 1980 the worker stopped scarfing entirely.  It was in the summer of 1981 that his arm and shoulder condition caused him to lay-off work for three months.  Reports by both an orthopaedist and the family doctor relating the tendonitis to scarfing were discounted since their factual bases were not consistent with that established in evidence before the Panel.

DecKeywords: Disability (disabled from working); Stress, mental (effect of disciplinary action)
DecSummary: Where it can be proven that stress at work results in disablement arising out of and in the course of employment, compensation will result.  The worker did feel stressed by the events surrounding his discharge after allegations of assault were made against him, reinstatement on a procedural point, and change of duties to a more highly supervised position.  But the panel found that he was not disabled by stress.  Whereas disablement refers to an inability to do work, either total or partial, the panel was convinced on the evidence that the worker could do his work during the periods in question, albeit with less productivity and energy than he might have wished.  He was not generally incapacitated since he was able to carry out his assigned job duties for months.  And the evidence disclosed no specific circumstances that made the days he laid off any different from all the other days he was able to work.

DecSummary: The worker's left index finger disability resulted from her work as a break down operator splicing film into 50 foot lengths by pressing a spring knife between 750 and 860 times a day.  She had no symptoms before she performed the job, pain slowly developed and got worse, and the joint near the end of the finger became crooked.  Co-workers confirmed her complaints and relation of the problem to her work.  The panel discounted a Board doctor's opinion that the disability was related not to the job but to multiple osteoarthritis since of the four osteoarthritis sites revealed by x-ray, only one was unrelated to injury or repetitive use, the arthritis at other sites was less advanced than in the index finger, and several medical opinions supported a work relationship.  Though the worker's age (then 57) and the several sites suggested she may have been susceptible to developing osteoarthritis, her work was a significant cause of the left index finger disability she actually developed.
